cases.title: Platform weekly sync
transcript: Okay, I think we're recording now. Can everyone hear me? Great. So this is the platform weekly, it's the 15th, and we've got about thirty minutes. Rebecca is out at the vendor conference in Denver this week, so we'll catch her up async, and I'll post notes in the channel afterwards. Jordan, thanks for recording this, it saves me from typing furiously. The agenda is pretty short: the log pipeline replacement, the failover game day, the billing service deploys, and then the budget for next quarter. If anything else comes up we can do it at the end. Theo, do you want to kick us off with the log pipeline, since you've been talking to vendors? Yeah, sure. So, quick recap for everybody: our current log pipeline is the self-hosted cluster we inherited from the analytics team, and it's costing us roughly nine thousand a month in storage alone, plus a lot of on-call pain.

I've had intro calls with five vendors so far. Two of them are basically out because they can't do data residency in the EU, which we need for the Oslo customers. Of the remaining three, the pricing models are all over the place: one charges per gigabyte ingested, one per host, and one has this credit system that I still don't fully understand. What I'd like to do is put together a proper vendor shortlist, the top two or three, with a side-by-side on cost at our current volume and at double our volume, plus the migration effort. Okay, that sounds right to me. When do you think you can have the shortlist? I can have it by Thursday. I'll put it in the shared drive and tag everyone. Great. Aisha, you had a question? Yeah, just, does the shortlist include the self-hosted option as a baseline? Because I think we should compare against keeping what we have and fixing it.

Good point, yes, I'll include keeping the current cluster as the baseline, with the cost of fixing the retention problem. Thanks. Kenji, anything on your side about logs? Only that the billing service is the noisiest producer by far, like forty percent of the volume is billing debug logs that nobody reads. So whatever we pick, we should turn those down first. That alone might cut the bill a lot. Okay, let's make that part of the billing work. Jordan, you've been quiet, anything from the incident side? Yeah, just one thing. During last Tuesday's outage the logs were delayed by almost twenty minutes, which is why it took us so long to find the bad deploy. So whatever we choose, ingestion latency needs to be one of the criteria, not just cost. Makes sense. Theo, can you add latency as a column? Yep, adding it now.

Okay, moving on to the failover game day. Aisha, this one's yours. Right, so the game day is scheduled for the 23rd, which is next Wednesday. The plan is to fail the primary database over to the secondary region during business hours, with customer support warned in advance, and see what breaks. The last time we did this, in March, the failover itself worked, but the runbook was badly out of date. Half the commands referenced the old cluster names, and the DNS step was just missing. So before the game day I'm going to update the failover runbook end to end and do a dry run on staging. Do you need anyone to review it? Yes, ideally someone who wasn't involved in writing it last time, so they'll notice what's unclear. I can review it, as long as I get it by Monday. Thanks Kenji, I'll send it to you Monday morning.

One more thing on the game day. We need someone from support on the bridge, and someone from the data team, because the analytics replicas will lag. Marisol, can you ask their managers? Yes, I'll ask both of them today. And are we telling customers? No, the plan is that it should be invisible to customers; if it isn't, that's exactly what we want to learn. But the status page should have a maintenance notice ready just in case. Who owns the status page draft? I'll do it, I did the last one. Okay, so Jordan drafts the status page notice. Fine. Is there anything that would make us cancel the game day? If there's an active incident that morning, or if the runbook dry run fails on staging. Let's agree on that: we go ahead on the 23rd unless there's an active incident or the staging dry run fails. Everyone okay with that? Yep. Sounds good.

Great. Billing service. Kenji. So the billing deploys have been painful. We've had two rollbacks in the last month, both because a config change that looked fine in staging broke invoicing for a subset of customers in production. The staging data just doesn't look like production for billing. What I want to do is set up a canary deploy for the billing service, so that every release goes to five percent of traffic first, and we watch the invoice error rate for thirty minutes before rolling out further. We already have the canary tooling for the API gateway, so it's mostly plumbing. How long? About a week of work, maybe a bit more, because the billing service still runs on the old deploy pipeline. Can you get it done before the end of the month? I think so, yes, if nothing else catches fire.

Does the canary need anything from the data side? Just the invoice error metric, which already exists, but it's only computed every fifteen minutes. I'd need it every minute for the canary to make sense. Okay, that's a dependency on the data team then. Theo, you have a good relationship with them, can you ask? Sure, I'll ask Priyanka about the metric frequency. Actually wait, I thought Priyanka moved to the forecasting team? She did, it's Samir now. Oh, right, then I'll ask Samir. Okay. Kenji, is this blocking? It's blocking the last step, the automated rollback, but I can build everything else first. Good. And the debug logs you mentioned earlier, turning those down, is that part of this? Yes, I'll fold that into the same change, it's a one-line config.

Okay, last agenda item: the budget for Q4. Finance wants every team's budget request by Friday. I've drafted ours: it's mostly the same as Q3, plus the observability vendor, whatever we pick, and two more on-call stipends because the rotation is getting thin. I'll send the Q4 budget to finance by Friday, but I need Theo's rough cost estimate from the shortlist before then, so Thursday really matters. I'll make sure the shortlist has a number you can use, even if it's a range. A range is fine. Also, Jordan, I want to include the training budget for the SRE course you asked about. What was the cost? It's about two thousand for the course plus travel. Okay, I'll put it in. Thanks, I appreciate that.

Anything else before we wrap? One thing from me. The on-call handoff document is out of date again. People keep asking in the channel who owns which alerts. We should really have one page with alert ownership. Agreed, but let's not take it on this week, everyone is already full. Let's put it on the list for next sync. Can someone just add it to the backlog so we don't forget? I'll add it to the backlog. Thanks Aisha. And Rebecca, when she's back, should hear about the game day, since she's the secondary for the database. I'll message her. Okay. So I think we're done a bit early, which never happens.

Let me read back the action items so they're on the recording. Theo: the vendor shortlist with cost at current and double volume, ingestion latency, and the self-hosted baseline, by Thursday. Aisha: update the failover runbook, do a staging dry run, and send it to Kenji for review on Monday. Kenji: the canary deploy for the billing service, including turning down the debug logs, before the end of the month, and review Aisha's runbook. Jordan: draft the status page maintenance notice for the game day. Me: send the Q4 budget to finance by Friday, and ask support and the data team for people on the game day bridge. And Theo also asks Samir about the invoice error metric. Did I miss anything? I think that's everything.

Great. Oh, one more question, is the game day still at ten in the morning? Yes, ten Pacific, and we'll block two hours. Okay, I'll put it in my calendar. Also, heads up, I'm out on Monday morning for a dentist appointment, so the runbook review will happen Monday afternoon when I'm back. That works, Kenji. Actually, one last thing about the vendors: one of them offered a free proof of concept for thirty days. Should I take that? Only after the shortlist. Let's not start a proof of concept with a vendor that might not make the cut. Makes sense, I'll tell them we'll get back to them next week.

Alright, thanks everyone, that was a good one. Jordan, can you stop the recording when we drop? Sure. Before I do, Marisol, do you want the notes in the channel or in the doc? The doc, please, and link it from the channel. Will do. Theo, good luck with the vendors, and Aisha, ping me if the staging dry run turns anything up before Monday. Will do. Okay, stopping the recording now. Thanks all. Bye. See you Thursday. Bye.

cases.title: Career chat: analytics to ML
transcript: Hi, can you hear me okay? Yes, perfect. Thanks so much for making time, Beatriz, I know your calendar is packed. Of course, happy to. Our mutual friend said you're thinking about moving from analytics into machine learning? Yes, exactly. So I've been a data analyst at a logistics company for about three years. I do a lot of SQL, dashboards, some forecasting in spreadsheets, and lately a bit of Python. And I keep ending up on projects where I think a model would help, but then someone else builds it. So I'd love to understand how you'd approach the switch, and what your team at Emberline Energy actually looks for when you hire. Sure. So, a bit of context about me first: I lead data science at Emberline, the team is twelve people, and about half of them came from analytics backgrounds, so this is a path I've seen work many times.

The honest answer is that the gap from analyst to ML engineer is less about algorithms and more about engineering habits. The people who make the switch successfully can take a model from a notebook to something that runs every day without them babysitting it. So version control, testing, writing code other people can read, basic deployment. The modeling part, at least for the kind of forecasting we do, is often simpler than people expect. Load forecasting, for example, is mostly gradient-boosted trees and very careful feature engineering on weather and calendar data. That's really reassuring, actually. I was worried I'd need to go back and do a master's. You don't, not for most applied roles. What I'd do instead is build one serious portfolio project end to end, and I'm happy to send you a reading list to go with it.

What would a good portfolio project look like? Something with real, messy data and a real deployment. Since you're in logistics, you could forecast something from public data, like hourly electricity demand for a region, which also happens to be what we do. Take the public demand data plus weather, build a forecast, evaluate it honestly against a simple baseline, and then deploy it so it produces a new forecast every day and writes it somewhere. Put the whole thing in a public repository with a short write-up of what didn't work. The write-up is the part hiring managers actually read. Okay, that's really concrete. So I'll build that portfolio project on electricity demand forecasting. How long should it take? If you do it evenings and weekends, maybe six to eight weeks. Don't polish it forever. Ship something rough first and iterate.

And on the reading list, what's on it? A couple of books on forecasting and on ML in production, and a few engineering blog posts from teams that do this at scale. I'll send you the reading list by the end of the week, and I'll mark which chapters to skip, because some of those books are long. That would be amazing. Also, and this is a bigger offer, once you have a draft of the project, I'd be happy to do a mock interview with you, the same format we use for our ML engineer loop: a project deep dive and a short modeling discussion. Wow, yes, I'd love that. Let's pencil the mock interview in for about three weeks from now, and if the project isn't ready, we'll just talk through what you have. Great, I'll send you a few times.

One more thing. You should meet Tomas Varga, who leads our ML platform team. He moved from analytics to engineering himself, maybe six years ago, and he's much better than me at explaining the engineering side, how we deploy and monitor models. I'll introduce you to Tomas over email this week. Thank you, that's really generous. Is Emberline hiring for these roles right now, by the way? Not at the moment for ML engineers; we just filled two positions. But we usually open new roles in the spring, and I'd rather you apply with the portfolio project done than rush now. That makes sense. And honestly, even if it's not Emberline, the project will help anywhere. Exactly.

Okay, I've taken a lot of your time. Let me recap so I don't forget: I'm building the portfolio project on electricity demand forecasting, you're sending the reading list by the end of the week, we'll do a mock interview in about three weeks, and you'll introduce me to Tomas. Did I get that right? That's it. And send me the repository link as soon as there's anything in it, even if it's messy. I will. Thank you so much, Beatriz, this was incredibly helpful. My pleasure, good luck, and talk soon. Bye. Bye.

cases.title: Insights Q4 planning workshop
transcript: Okay, it says recording. Casey, you're recording on your side too, right? Great, thank you. So welcome, everyone, to the Insights Q4 planning workshop. We've got the whole afternoon blocked, but I'd love to finish a bit early if we can. For anyone who hasn't seen the agenda, we're going to do five blocks. First, Soo-ah walks us through the Q3 numbers. Second, Amani shares the customer research readout from the interviews in August and September. Third, Rui takes us through the Heron migration, which is the big engineering bet for the quarter. Fourth, Felix has the pricing and packaging proposal. And then at the end we'll do team stuff: the offsite, hiring, and a few loose ends. I'll keep time and try to capture decisions in the planning doc as we go, and Casey's recording will be the backup for anything I miss. Does that sound okay to everyone? Any changes to the agenda? And before anyone asks, yes, there are snacks, and yes, we'll take a proper break halfway through, probably after Amani's section, so people can refill coffee and check messages.

Just one small request from me. Could we do pricing before Heron? I have to drop for about twenty minutes around three for a customer call, and I'd rather not miss the pricing discussion since it's mine. Hmm, Rui, would that work for you? Honestly I'd prefer to keep Heron earlier, because some of the pricing ideas depend on what the new backend can do, like the usage-based stuff. Right, that's fair. Felix, what if we keep the order, and if Heron runs long, we pause it when you step out, do the team topics, and come back to pricing when you're back? Yeah, that works. Okay, good. And one more housekeeping thing: the planning doc is linked in the invite, so please add comments there rather than in the chat, because chat gets lost. Right. Soo-ah, over to you for the Q3 numbers. And please interrupt her with questions as we go, I'd rather we clear up confusion in the moment than save it all for the end.

Thanks, Helga. Okay, let me share my screen. Can everyone see the dashboard? Yes. Okay. So, headline numbers for Q3. We ended the quarter with just under two thousand four hundred paying accounts, which is up eleven percent from Q2. Net revenue retention came in at one hundred and four percent, which is fine but lower than the one hundred and ten we had in the first half of the year. The main driver of that dip is contraction, not churn: customers are keeping us, but they're downgrading seats, especially in the mid-market segment. Logo churn was actually flat at about one point eight percent a month. So the story is less that people are leaving and more that people are using us less and paying for fewer seats. I'll show the breakdown by segment in a second, because it's really one segment driving all of this. Quick question before you switch: is the one hundred and four percent calculated on the same cohort as last quarter? Yes, same methodology, trailing twelve months, so the comparison is apples to apples.

Here's the segment view. Enterprise is healthy, basically no contraction, and they're the ones asking for the streaming features. SMB is noisy as always, a lot of accounts come and go, but they're small. The problem is mid-market, the accounts with between fifty and five hundred employees. Seat contraction there was about six percent over the quarter. When we look at usage, the median mid-market account opened a dashboard on only nine days in September, down from thirteen in June. Sorry, can I ask, when you say opened a dashboard, does that include the scheduled email reports? Because a lot of mid-market customers just read the emailed PDF and never log in. No, it doesn't. That's a good point. The emailed reports are counted separately, and actually email report opens went up over the same period, by about fifteen percent.

So that's interesting, right? Maybe they're not using us less, they're just using us differently. Could be. That's partly why I wanted to bring up definitions today, because right now we have three different definitions of an active account floating around. Product uses logged in at least once in the last thirty days. Finance uses had any billable usage in the month, which includes the email reports. And the board deck uses weekly active users divided by seats, which is a completely different thing. So depending on which one you pick, mid-market engagement is either down twenty percent or up five percent. Oof. Yeah. And the board deck is the one everyone quotes. Which is also the one that makes mid-market look worst, because seats are exactly what they're cutting. So we're kind of measuring the symptom and calling it the disease. And to be fair to whoever built the board deck, that metric made sense two years ago, when almost every seat was a person who logged in every day. It just hasn't aged well.

Okay, this feels like something we need to fix before we set any Q4 targets, otherwise we'll argue about the target forever. Agreed. Soo-ah, what would it take to settle on one definition? Honestly, a short document that lists our core metrics, active account, active user, retention, contraction, with one definition each, how it's computed, and which table it comes from. A metrics glossary, basically. Then we get finance and product to sign off on it once. I love that. Can you own it? Yes, I can draft the metrics glossary. I'd want Felix to review the revenue definitions and Rui to check the table names. Happy to. When could you have a draft? Let's say two weeks, so before the October 23rd leadership review. Perfect, that's the deadline then: glossary draft before the leadership review on October 23rd.

One more thing on the numbers before we move on. The activation rate for new trials dropped too, from thirty-one percent to twenty-six percent. Activation meaning they connected a data source and built a first dashboard in their first week. That coincides with the new onboarding flow we shipped in August, so it might be the flow, or it might be seasonality, because August trials are always a bit weird with people on vacation. Do we have a holdout? No, we shipped it to everyone. Hmm. Okay, so we can't really tell. Not with confidence. I can compare against last August, but that's about it. Let's note that as an open question. I don't want us to jump to reverting the onboarding flow without data. Can you add it to the planning doc under open questions? Done, it's in there now. I also added a note that we should never ship an onboarding change without a holdout again, because this is the second time we've been stuck guessing afterwards.

Anything else on the Q3 numbers? Just a quick question: the revenue number you showed, is that recognized revenue or bookings? Recognized. Bookings were a bit higher because of the two annual enterprise renewals in September. Got it, thanks. And I think the mid-market contraction is going to come up again in the research readout, because a lot of the interviews were with mid-market customers. Yeah, it definitely will. Okay, great. Thank you, Soo-ah, that was really clear, and I appreciate you pulling the email report numbers, that changes the picture. Let's move on to Amani, who is going to walk us through the customer research. Amani, you've got about twenty-five minutes, but take what you need. Thanks. Let me grab the screen. Okay, can you see the slides? Yes. Great. So, some context first. This was the biggest research round we've done since I joined, so I want to explain how we picked people before I get into what they said.

Between mid-August and mid-September we did fourteen customer interviews. Nine mid-market, three enterprise, two SMB. We specifically recruited accounts that had contracted seats in the last six months, plus a few healthy ones as a comparison. Each interview was forty-five minutes, and Casey sat in on about half of them, thank you, Casey, which helped a lot with the note-taking. I've grouped what we heard into four themes. I'll go through each one with a couple of quotes, and then I'll talk about what I think we should do next. And I want to flag up front: fourteen interviews is enough to find themes, it's not enough to size them. So please treat everything I say as directional. I'll come back to how we size it at the end, because that's where I need help from this group. Also, all the recordings and my raw notes are in the research folder if anyone wants to listen to the full interviews, and I'd honestly recommend at least two of them for everyone on this call.

Theme one: reports are too slow. This came up in eleven of the fourteen interviews. People described opening a dashboard in the morning and seeing yesterday's numbers, and then having to wait for the nightly refresh to see anything from today. One operations lead said, and I'm quoting, by the time your dashboard tells me something is wrong, my team has already told me in chat. That's a pretty brutal quote. Another customer said they export to spreadsheets every morning and rebuild the numbers themselves because they don't trust the timing. So there's a freshness problem, and it's feeding a trust problem. And honestly this connects directly to Heron, which is why I'm glad Rui is presenting right after me. If Heron makes the numbers fresh, a lot of this theme goes away on its own. Did anyone say how fresh is fresh enough? Most said within the hour would be fine. Only two, both in operations, really wanted it within a few minutes.

Theme two: exports are confusing. Eight people mentioned it. The PDF exports and the CSV exports don't match, because the PDF uses the dashboard's filters and the CSV uses the raw query. People send the PDF to their boss and the CSV to their analyst, and then the two of them come back with different numbers and it becomes a whole thing. One finance manager told us she had to explain to her CFO why our product showed two different revenue figures for the same week. That kind of thing is exactly what makes a champion stop defending us internally. Oh no. Yeah. And the fix might be pretty small, right? Just make the CSV respect the filters? Probably, but I'd want Rui's team to confirm before we promise anything to customers.

Theme three: people want alerts, not dashboards. This is the one I find most interesting. Seven people, mostly the ones who contracted seats, said something like, I don't want to look at a dashboard, I want you to tell me when something changes. They're cutting seats for people who used to log in to check numbers, and replacing that with basically nothing, or with one analyst who checks and forwards things. If we had alerts, those people might actually stay on as lightweight users. So one hypothesis is that the seat contraction isn't because they don't value the data, it's because our product assumes everyone wants to come and look, and a lot of people just want to be told. That's a big claim, though. It is, which is why I want to test it properly before we build anything. I'll also say the people who described this were not the loudest customers, they were quiet ones who mostly read the emailed reports, which is probably why we haven't heard it in support tickets.

Theme four is smaller: onboarding. Four of the newer customers said the setup was confusing, specifically the step where you connect a data source and pick which tables to sync. Two of them said they almost gave up. This lines up with the activation drop Soo-ah mentioned, though it's only four people, so again, directional. Okay, so those are the four themes: slow reports, confusing exports, alerts instead of dashboards, and onboarding friction. What I'd propose next is a quantitative survey to size these. We have the beta cohort of about three hundred accounts who opted into research, and I'd send them a short survey, ten questions, asking them to rank these problems and tell us how they currently get the information they need.

When would the survey go out? I'd like to send the survey to the beta cohort in the first week of November, so we have results before we finalize the first-half roadmap in December. Can it go earlier? The planning cycle is tight. It could go at the end of October at the earliest, but I need a week to write it and get it reviewed, and I'd like Soo-ah to help me with the sampling so we don't over-represent the happy customers. Sure, I can help with that. Okay, so Amani owns the survey, with help from Soo-ah on sampling, and it goes out the first week of November. And please include a question about the email reports, given what Soo-ah found about email report opens going up. Good call, I'll add that. I'll share the draft questions in the planning doc next week. If anyone has a question they've always wanted to ask customers, add it there, but I'll be ruthless about keeping it to ten questions, because response rates fall off a cliff after that.

Questions for Amani before we move on? Just one. On the alerts theme, did anyone mention a specific channel? Email, chat, text messages? Mostly email and chat. Nobody asked for text messages. A couple of enterprise customers asked for webhooks so they can pipe alerts into their own incident tools. Okay, interesting. That's probably a much bigger build. Yeah, I'd treat webhooks as a later thing. One more question: did the exports theme come up with enterprise too, or just mid-market? Mostly mid-market. Enterprise customers mostly use the API directly. Right, makes sense. Great, thank you, Amani, this was really useful. I think a lot of what we just heard is going to shape the next hour. Rui, do you want to take it from here with Heron?

Sure. So, Heron. For people newer to the team, Heron is the codename for migrating our reporting backend from the nightly batch jobs to a streaming architecture. Right now every dashboard number is computed by a set of batch jobs that run at two in the morning and take about three hours. That's why the numbers are always yesterday's. Heron replaces that with a streaming pipeline, so events get processed within a couple of minutes and dashboards can show today's numbers. It also, and this is important for Felix's pricing discussion, gives us a real-time usage count per account, which we don't have today, because today usage is also computed in the nightly batch. So Heron is both a customer-facing feature and an internal enabler for billing. I'll go through where we are, the risks, what I'm proposing for Q4, and what I need from this group. Stop me if anything is unclear, some of this gets technical fast.

Where are we? We did a spike in Q3. Two engineers spent about six weeks building a prototype for one dashboard type, the revenue overview, on the new pipeline. It worked: end-to-end latency was under ninety seconds at our current volume. But we found three big risks. First, backfills. When a customer changes a metric definition, we need to recompute history, and streaming systems are bad at that. We'll need a hybrid, streaming for new data and batch for backfills. Second, cost. Our estimate is that the streaming infrastructure costs about forty percent more per month than the batch jobs, at least at first. Third, and this is the one that worries me most, the migration itself. We have about sixty dashboard types, and each one has its own quirks. Some of them have custom SQL that customers wrote years ago, and we don't even fully know what it does. Those are the scary ones.

How long do you think the full migration takes? Honestly, if we do all sixty dashboard types, two quarters with the current team. That's too long. I agree. So my proposal is to not migrate everything. We look at which dashboard types drive the most usage and the most complaints about freshness, and we do those first. From the usage data, twelve dashboard types account for about eighty percent of views. If we migrate those twelve in Q4, most customers would see today's numbers most of the time. And the long tail stays on batch until Q1 or Q2. That sounds much more reasonable. Does the hybrid approach mean some dashboards will show fresh numbers and others won't? Yes, and we'd need to show a freshness label on each dashboard so people aren't confused.

I'm a bit worried about that from a research point of view. If half the dashboards are fresh and half aren't, customers might trust the whole product less, not more. That's exactly the trust problem from the interviews. Hmm, fair. What if the label is really clear, like updated two minutes ago versus updated this morning at two a.m.? Then at least they know what they're looking at. That could work. Honestly, the worst thing today is that there's no label at all, so people don't know whether the numbers are stale. Even a label on the batch dashboards would help. Oh, that's a good point. We could ship the freshness label on the existing dashboards right away, before Heron, it's basically free. I like that. Let's note that as a quick win in the doc. Amani, would you want to test the label wording with a couple of customers first? Yes, I can do quick five-minute tests with people from the interview pool, they already said they're happy to be contacted again.

Okay, staffing. To migrate the twelve dashboard types in Q4, I need the two engineers from the spike full time, plus one more backend engineer for about half the quarter, plus someone from Soo-ah's team to validate that the numbers match between the old and new pipelines. Validation is the part people always underestimate. If the new numbers are off by even half a percent, customers will notice, and then we're back to the trust problem. I can give you someone for validation, but not full time. Maybe two days a week. Two days a week is probably enough if we set up automated comparisons. And the extra backend engineer? That would have to come from the integrations team, which means slowing down the new connectors. That's a trade-off for Helga to make, not me. I'll just say that without the third engineer, twelve dashboard types becomes more like eight in Q4, and the rest slips into January.

Yeah, let me think about that one. My instinct is that freshness matters more than new connectors this quarter, given everything Amani showed us. But I want to talk to the integrations lead before deciding, because they have commitments to two enterprise customers. Let's put that down as an open decision, and I'll come back with an answer by Friday. Okay. And the cost, the forty percent increase, is that in the budget? Not yet. That's the other thing I need: sign-off on the infrastructure budget increase for Heron. Do you have a number? About eleven thousand a month more at current volume, going down to maybe six thousand once we turn off the batch jobs for the migrated dashboards. Okay, that's not crazy. Put it in the plan and I'll take it to finance.

So what do you need from us to move forward? Mainly, I want to write up a proper Heron migration plan: the twelve dashboard types in order, the hybrid architecture for backfills, the validation approach, the staffing, the cost, and the rollout, which I think should be behind a feature flag per account so we can start with internal accounts and a few friendly customers. When can you have the plan? I'll write the Heron migration plan by October 30th. That gives me time to talk to the integrations lead with Helga, and to get cost estimates from the infrastructure team. Perfect. And please include the freshness label as phase zero, since we said that can ship right away. Will do, phase zero is the freshness label on the existing dashboards.

Any other questions on Heron? One from me: does Heron change anything for the exports problem Amani described? Partly. If exports are generated from the same pipeline as the dashboards, the PDF and the CSV should match automatically for the migrated dashboard types. But for the batch ones, we'd still need the quick fix to make the CSV respect the filters. Can we just do the quick fix for everything now? Probably, it's maybe a week of work. But let me confirm, I don't want to promise it before I've looked at the code. Okay. Let's put the export fix down as a candidate quick win, pending Rui checking the effort. Sounds good. Alright, Felix, I think you're up next with pricing. Do you still have to drop at three? I do, but we have about twenty-five minutes, so let's go.

Great. So, pricing and packaging. The short version: our pricing today is almost entirely per seat. Customers pay for every person who can log in.
